feedback: For a wrong classification, re-anchor to the nervous-system effect: does the drug slow signals (depressant), speed them up (stimulant) or distort perception (hallucinogen)?
For a dependence item, remind: physical = body adapts and withdrawal appears; psychological = craving/compulsion.
activities.intendedInsight: Secure recall of the classification and specific organ harms, and of the physical/psychological dependence distinction.
learnerActions: Categorise named drugs as depressant, stimulant or hallucinogen.
Match each drug to the main organ(s) it harms (e.g. alcohol → liver/brain; tobacco → lungs/heart).
Answer items distinguishing physical from psychological dependence.
activities.title: Classification and drug→organ check

feedback: If a learner expects alcohol to 'speed you up', the model shows a lengthened reaction time, reinforcing that a depressant slows signalling.
activities.intendedInsight: Makes the mechanism felt: 'depressant' and 'stimulant' describe slowing or speeding of nervous-system signalling, which drives the behavioural effects.
learnerActions: Explore a simple model of nervous-system signal transmission where a depressant lengthens reaction time and a stimulant shortens it.
Compare the modelled reaction time for a depressant versus a stimulant and connect it to real behaviour (e.g. why alcohol impairs reactions).
activities.title: Optional reaction-time / synapse mini-model
